items.title: Natural Law has primary and secondary precepts
items.claim: What are Aquinas's primary precepts of natural law?

options.text: Five primary precepts identified by Aquinas: preservation of life, reproduction, education of offspring, living in society, worship of God — secondary precepts (specific moral rules) are derived from them by reason
A single rule: do good and avoid evil

items.reveal:
Aquinas's natural law theory appears in the Summa Theologiae I-II (Questions 90-97). The eternal law is God's plan; natural law is rational creatures' participation in it; human law derives specific rules.

The doctrine of double effect — an action with a foreseen bad consequence can be permissible if the bad effect is not intended, the act itself is not intrinsically wrong, and the good outweighs the bad — is a key application (used in modern bioethics).

Natural law is the basis of Catholic moral teaching on contraception, abortion and end-of-life care. John Finnis and Germain Grisez developed 'New Natural Law' (from 1980) updating the framework.
items.why: Catholic ethics is not arbitrary doctrine — it rests on a developed rational framework. Engaging with natural law requires understanding the structure (primary, secondary, double effect) rather than treating it as a list of forbidden actions.

items.title: Aquinas offered five arguments for God, not one

options.text: Five distinct arguments from observation: motion (unmoved mover), causation (uncaused cause), contingency (necessary being), degree (greatest being), teleology (designer) — in Summa Theologiae I.2.3

items.reveal:
Aquinas distinguishes 'a priori' arguments (from concept to existence — Anselm's ontological) from 'a posteriori' arguments (from observation). His Five Ways are all a posteriori — they begin from empirical features of the world.

First Way (motion): things move and change; an unmoved mover is required to start the chain. Second Way (efficient causation): everything has a cause; a first cause is required. Third Way (contingency): contingent things require a necessary being. Fourth Way (degree): degrees of perfection require a maximum. Fifth Way (teleology): purposive ordering requires a designer.

Each has been criticised individually. Hume and Kant attacked the cosmological framework; Darwinian biology challenges the teleological reading; Russell's response to Copleston challenged the contingency argument.
items.why: Aquinas is sometimes reduced to a single 'cosmological argument'. He offered five distinct arguments that need to be evaluated separately — and Catholic natural theology still rests on this framework.
